Reliability of deprivation indices: omega, model fit and misclassification

Simulated consensual deprivation data with lavaan and semTools

22 October 2026

1 Purpose and workflow

This document shows how to assess the reliability of a multiple deprivation index with confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and the omega coefficient. Two ten-item indices are measured for the same 10,000 simulated people:

  • Index A. Ten items widely endorsed as necessities under the consensual approach.
  • Index B. An alternative ten-item index for the same population that combines relative deprivation items with unsatisfied basic needs (UBN) indicators, as in many Latin American poverty measures.

The comparison between indices uses one-factor (unidimensional) models, which is the model implied when items are added up into a single count. A two-factor model for Index B is also fitted to see whether one dimension is enough.

Steps:

  1. Load the data (simulated from a known true deprivation score).
  2. Describe both indices.
  3. Fit and compare CFA models (chi-square, CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR) and draw them as path diagrams.
  4. Inspect factor loadings and item R².
  5. Examine item severity and information.
  6. Estimate omega.
  7. Relate factor scores to simple sum scores.
  8. Show what high and low measurement error does to scores.
  9. Quantify misclassification of the poor.

Required packages: lavaan (0.6-13 or later), semTools, semPlot, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, knitr.

library(lavaan)
library(semTools)
library(semPlot)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
pal <- c("Index A" = "#1b6ca8", "Index B" = "#c0392b")

2 Data

Two files are needed:

  • deprivation_data.csv: one row per person with id, the true deprivation score eta, and the binary items of both indices. Relative deprivation items are coded 1 = lacks the item because they cannot afford it; UBN items are coded 1 = the condition is present.
  • item_dictionary.csv: index, item code and label.

Each person has a true deprivation score eta ~ N(0, 1). Binary items come from a latent response y* = loading × eta + error and are coded 1 when y* exceeds a threshold fixed by the item’s prevalence. Some items also depend on characteristics of the household or its surroundings other than deprivation. The column eta is known only because the data are simulated; the sections on scores, measurement error and misclassification use it.

Set the paths in the YAML header (params) or render with rmarkdown::render("omega_deprivation.Rmd", params = list(data_file = "...", items_file = "...")).

dat   <- read.csv(params$data_file)
items <- read.csv(params$items_file)

items_A <- subset(items, index == "A")
items_B <- subset(items, index == "B")

stopifnot(all(c("eta", items$item) %in% names(dat)),
          all(unlist(dat[, items$item]) %in% c(0, 1)))

A <- as.matrix(dat[, items_A$item])
B <- as.matrix(dat[, items_B$item])

dat$score_A <- rowSums(A)
dat$score_B <- rowSums(B)

c(people = nrow(dat), items_A = ncol(A), items_B = ncol(B))
##  people items_A items_B 
##   10000      10      10

3.2 Deprivation scores

The simple score is the count of items lacked (0 to 10).

alpha_coef <- function(x) {
  k <- ncol(x)
  k / (k - 1) * (1 - sum(apply(x, 2, var)) / var(rowSums(x)))
}

scores_long <- dat %>%
  select(score_A, score_B) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "index", values_to = "score") %>%
  mutate(index = recode(index, score_A = "Index A", score_B = "Index B"))

desc <- scores_long %>%
  group_by(index) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(score), sd = sd(score), median = median(score),
            p_zero = mean(score == 0), p_3plus = mean(score >= 3),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(alpha = c(alpha_coef(A), alpha_coef(B)))

kable(desc, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Index", "Mean", "SD", "Median", "Share 0", "Share 3+", "Alpha"))
Index Mean SD Median Share 0 Share 3+ Alpha
Index A 1.75 2.44 1 0.45 0.25 0.85
Index B 1.76 1.83 1 0.32 0.28 0.69 
ggplot(scores_long, aes(score, fill = index)) +
  geom_bar(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(x = "Number of deprivations", y = "People", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Alpha is reported for reference only; with binary items the model-based omega below is the preferred coefficient.

4 Model evaluation and comparison

Items are declared as ordered, so lavaan uses polychoric correlations and the WLSMV estimator. Report the scaled (robust) statistics. Usual benchmarks: CFI and TLI ≥ .95, RMSEA ≤ .06, SRMR ≤ .08. With n = 10,000 the chi-square test rejects almost any model, so it is read together with the fit indices.

Three models are fitted:

  • A-1F: one deprivation factor for Index A.
  • B-1F: one deprivation factor for Index B (the model implied by summing the items).
  • B-2F: two correlated factors for Index B, estimated without deciding in advance which items go with which factor (exploratory structure inside lavaan, geomin rotation).

Model syntax in lavaan:

  • =~ reads “is measured by”: the latent factor on the left, its items on the right.
  • efa("b")*F1 + efa("b")*F2 =~ ... defines two factors in the same exploratory block "b": every item loads on both factors and the solution is rotated.
  • ordered = lists the binary items, so they are treated as categorical.
  • std.lv = TRUE fixes factor variances to 1, so all loadings are estimated.
# A-1F: one factor, Index A
m_A1 <- '
  dep =~ a_meals + a_shoes + a_coat + a_fruitveg + a_damp +
         a_warm + a_medicine + a_savings + a_celebrate + a_appliances
'

# B-1F: one factor, Index B
m_B1 <- '
  dep =~ b_fruitveg + b_dirtfloor + b_warm + b_learning + b_childdeath +
         b_savings + b_violence + b_water + b_celebrate + b_educ
'

# B-2F: two correlated factors, Index B, exploratory loadings
m_B2 <- '
  efa("b")*F1 +
  efa("b")*F2 =~ b_fruitveg + b_dirtfloor + b_warm + b_learning + b_childdeath +
                 b_savings + b_violence + b_water + b_celebrate + b_educ
'

ord_A <- c("a_meals", "a_shoes", "a_coat", "a_fruitveg", "a_damp",
           "a_warm", "a_medicine", "a_savings", "a_celebrate", "a_appliances")
ord_B <- c("b_fruitveg", "b_dirtfloor", "b_warm", "b_learning", "b_childdeath",
           "b_savings", "b_violence", "b_water", "b_celebrate", "b_educ")

fit_A1 <- cfa(m_A1, data = dat, ordered = ord_A, std.lv = TRUE)
fit_B1 <- cfa(m_B1, data = dat, ordered = ord_B, std.lv = TRUE)
fit_B2 <- cfa(m_B2, data = dat, ordered = ord_B, std.lv = TRUE,
              rotation = "geomin")

fit_tab <- function(fit, name) {
  fm <- fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq.scaled", "df.scaled", "pvalue.scaled",
                           "cfi.scaled", "tli.scaled", "rmsea.scaled", "srmr"))
  data.frame(model = name, as.list(round(unclass(fm), 3)))
}

fits <- rbind(fit_tab(fit_A1, "A-1F"), fit_tab(fit_B1, "B-1F"), fit_tab(fit_B2, "B-2F"))
kable(fits, col.names = c("Model", "Chi-sq", "df", "p", "CFI", "TLI", "RMSEA", "SRMR"))

B-1F 2754.603 35 0 0.900 0.871 0.088 0.127
B-2F 444.687 26 0 0.985 0.973 0.040 0.051

The largest modification indices of the one-factor models locate the sources of misfit (residual correlations between pairs of items).

mi_top <- function(fit, name) {
  modindices(fit, sort. = TRUE, maximum.number = 5) %>%
    filter(op == "~~") %>%
    transmute(model = name, pair = paste(lhs, rhs, sep = " ~~ "), mi, sepc.all)
}
kable(rbind(mi_top(fit_A1, "A-1F"), mi_top(fit_B1, "B-1F")), digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Model", "Pair", "MI", "Std. residual correlation"))
Model Pair MI Std. residual correlation
A-1F a_damp a_warm 163.62 -0.74
A-1F a_fruitveg a_warm 10.86 0.13
A-1F a_shoes a_damp 9.70 0.26
A-1F a_warm a_medicine 8.40 0.13
A-1F a_warm a_savings 7.94 0.10
B-1F b_learning b_violence 1184.97 -0.65
B-1F b_savings b_celebrate 625.33 -2.18
B-1F b_savings b_violence 173.52 0.67
B-1F b_learning b_savings 151.24 0.58
B-1F b_fruitveg b_warm 148.44 -0.39

Interpretation:

  • A-1F: CFI = 0.995, TLI = 0.994, RMSEA = 0.028. The main misfit is a residual correlation between two housing items, a common and minor form of local dependence.
  • B-1F: CFI = 0.9, TLI = 0.871, RMSEA = 0.088, with a larger chi-square for the same degrees of freedom. The modification indices show which items share variance not explained by the deprivation factor.
  • B-2F: CFI = 0.985, TLI = 0.973, RMSEA = 0.04, with a factor correlation of 0.39. The loading table shows which items form each factor and which items load weakly on both. When a second factor does not bring the fit up to the benchmarks, the problem is not only dimensionality: several items share variance unrelated to deprivation and carry little information about it. Adding factors does not repair poor indicators, and Index B is still reported as a single count, which assumes one factor.
  • Fit indices tell whether a model reproduces the correlations. They do not tell how much of the score is error, which is why loadings and omega are examined next, using the one-factor models.

4.1 Path diagrams

The diagrams show standardised estimates. Circles are latent variables, squares are the observed items, single-headed arrows are loadings and the curved double-headed arrow is the factor correlation. Item labels are in the prevalence table. In B-2F, loadings below .30 are hidden to make the structure readable.

draw_path <- function(fit, main, minimum = 0) {
  semPaths(fit, what = "std", whatLabels = "std", layout = "tree",
           intercepts = FALSE, thresholds = FALSE, residuals = FALSE,
           minimum = minimum, color = list(lat = "#ffffff", man = "#dde8f3"),
           sizeMan = 7, sizeLat = 11, label.cex = 1, edge.label.cex = 0.85,
           edge.color = "grey25", edge.label.position = 0.55,
           nCharNodes = 0, mar = c(6, 3, 7, 3))
  title(main, line = 2.5, font.main = 1, cex.main = 1.1)
}
draw_path(fit_A1, "A-1F: one factor, Index A")

draw_path(fit_B1, "B-1F: one factor, Index B")

draw_path(fit_B2, "B-2F: two correlated factors, Index B", minimum = 0.30)

5 Factor loadings and R²

Loadings come from the one-factor models A-1F and B-1F. Standardised loadings show how strongly each item reflects deprivation. R² is the share of the item’s latent response variance explained by the factor (the squared loading in a one-factor model), and 1 - R² is the share that is error. Loadings below about .50 (R² below .25) signal weak indicators.

std_tab <- function(fit, items, index) {
  standardizedSolution(fit) %>%
    filter(op == "=~", lhs == "dep") %>%
    select(item = rhs, loading = est.std, se) %>%
    mutate(r2 = loading^2, index = index) %>%
    left_join(items %>% select(item, label), by = "item")
}

load_all <- bind_rows(
  std_tab(fit_A1, items_A, "Index A"),
  std_tab(fit_B1, items_B, "Index B")
)

Items with low R² add mostly error to the count. Their labels help judge whether they are valid indicators of deprivation in the first place.

6 Severity and item information

Loadings are not the only source of error. An item that only very deprived people lack (high severity) separates the most deprived from everyone else, but says almost nothing about differences in the rest of the population. With binary items this is read from the standardised thresholds of the one-factor models, converted to the item response theory (IRT) metric:

  • discrimination a = λ / sqrt(1 - λ²)
  • severity b = τ / λ, the point on the deprivation scale where the probability of being deprived is .50
  • item information I(θ) = a² φ(z)² / [Φ(z)(1 - Φ(z))], with z = a(θ - b)

Test information is the sum of item information; its inverse square root is the standard error of measurement at each level of deprivation.

irt_tab <- function(fit, items, index) {
  ss  <- standardizedSolution(fit)
  lam <- ss %>% filter(op == "=~") %>% select(item = rhs, loading = est.std)
  tau <- ss %>% filter(op == "|") %>% select(item = lhs, threshold = est.std)
  lam %>%
    left_join(tau, by = "item") %>%
    mutate(index = index,
           a = loading / sqrt(1 - loading^2),
           b = threshold / loading) %>%
    left_join(items %>% select(item, label), by = "item")
}

irt_all <- bind_rows(irt_tab(fit_A1, items_A, "Index A"),
                     irt_tab(fit_B1, items_B, "Index B"))

kable(irt_all %>% select(index, item, label, loading, threshold, a, b), digits = 2,

theta <- seq(-3, 4, by = 0.05)
info <- irt_all %>%
  tidyr::crossing(theta = theta) %>%
  mutate(z = a * (theta - b),
         info = a^2 * dnorm(z)^2 / (pnorm(z) * (1 - pnorm(z))))
info %>%
  group_by(index, theta) %>%
  summarise(info = sum(info), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(theta, info, colour = index)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(x = "Deprivation (θ)", y = "Test information", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

ggplot(info, aes(theta, info, group = item)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(data = info %>% group_by(item) %>% slice_max(info, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE),
            aes(label = item), size = 3, vjust = -0.4, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ index) +
  labs(x = "Deprivation (θ)", y = "Item information")

Items with high severity concentrate their information at the far right of the scale. Items with low discrimination have flat, low curves wherever they are located. Both add little to the measurement of most of the population, while still adding their error to the count.

7 Reliability: omega

Omega is the proportion of total score variance due to the common factor:

\[\omega = \frac{(\sum \lambda_i)^2}{(\sum \lambda_i)^2 + \sum \theta_{ii}}\]

For binary items, semTools::compRelSEM() returns the categorical omega of Green and Yang (2009), which refers to the observed sum score rather than the latent responses. Values around .80 or higher are usually considered adequate for an index used to classify people.

omega_tab <- data.frame(
  model = c("A-1F", "B-1F"),
  omega = c(compRelSEM(fit_A1), compRelSEM(fit_B1))
)
kable(omega_tab, digits = 3, col.names = c("Model", "Omega"))
Model Omega
A-1F 0.860
B-1F 0.772

Index A reaches omega = 0.86 and Index B 0.77. Both have ten items, so the difference comes from the quality of the indicators, not from the length of the index.

8 Factor scores and simple scores

In practice most indices are reported as counts. The question is how well the count tracks the factor score and, since the data are simulated, the true deprivation.

dat$fs_A <- as.numeric(lavPredict(fit_A1))
dat$fs_B <- as.numeric(lavPredict(fit_B1))

cor_tab <- data.frame(
  index = names(pal),
  r_sum_fs   = c(cor(dat$score_A, dat$fs_A), cor(dat$score_B, dat$fs_B)),
  rho_sum_fs = c(cor(dat$score_A, dat$fs_A, method = "spearman"),
                 cor(dat$score_B, dat$fs_B, method = "spearman")),
  r_sum_true = c(cor(dat$score_A, dat$eta), cor(dat$score_B, dat$eta)),
  r_fs_true  = c(cor(dat$fs_A, dat$eta), cor(dat$fs_B, dat$eta))
)
kable(cor_tab, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Index", "r (sum, factor)", "rho (sum, factor)",
                    "r (sum, true)", "r (factor, true)"))
Index r (sum, factor) rho (sum, factor) r (sum, true) r (factor, true)
Index A 0.963 0.995 0.806 0.838
Index B 0.958 0.971 0.719 0.748 
long_fs <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(index = names(pal)[1], score = dat$score_A, fs = dat$fs_A),
  data.frame(index = names(pal)[2], score = dat$score_B, fs = dat$fs_B)
)

ggplot(long_fs, aes(factor(score), fs, fill = index)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.4, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ index) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Deprivation score (count)", y = "Factor score")

Both counts correlate highly with their own factor scores, so a high correlation between sum and factor scores is not evidence of a good index. Within each count, factor scores vary because the model weights items by their loadings and thresholds. When an index mixes strong and weak items, lacking two strong items places a person much higher than lacking two weak ones, but the count treats both cases the same.

9 Low error versus high error

The squared correlation between an observed score and the true score is close to its reliability. The plot shows the true deprivation of people at each count. With low error each additional deprivation moves people clearly up the true scale. With high error the distributions overlap and the count says little about where a person really is.

long_true <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(index = names(pal)[1], score = dat$score_A, eta = dat$eta),
  data.frame(index = names(pal)[2], score = dat$score_B, eta = dat$eta)
)

ggplot(long_true, aes(factor(score), eta, fill = index)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.4, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ index) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Deprivation score (count)", y = "True deprivation")

long_true %>%
  group_by(index) %>%
  summarise(r2_true = cor(score, eta)^2,
            sd_true_within_score = mean(tapply(eta, score, sd), na.rm = TRUE))
## # A tibble: 2 × 3
##   index   r2_true sd_true_within_score
##   <chr>     <dbl>                <dbl>
## 1 Index A   0.650                0.396
## 2 Index B   0.517                0.594

10 Misclassification

Suppose the truly poor are the 20% with the highest true deprivation. Each index classifies people as poor using the count threshold that yields a prevalence closest to 20%, so both indices are compared at a similar poverty rate.

true_poor <- dat$eta > quantile(dat$eta, 0.80)

pick_cut <- function(score, target = 0.20) {
  ks <- 1:10
  ks[which.min(abs(sapply(ks, function(k) mean(score >= k)) - target))]
}

classify <- function(score, index) {
  k <- pick_cut(score)
  obs_poor <- score >= k
  data.frame(
    index = index, cutoff = k, prevalence = mean(obs_poor),
    sensitivity = mean(obs_poor[true_poor]),
    specificity = mean(!obs_poor[!true_poor]),
    false_pos = mean(obs_poor & !true_poor),
    false_neg = mean(!obs_poor & true_poor),
    misclassified = mean(obs_poor != true_poor)
  )
}

mis <- rbind(classify(dat$score_A, names(pal)[1]),
             classify(dat$score_B, names(pal)[2]))
kable(mis, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Index", "Cut-off", "Poor (%)", "Sensitivity", "Specificity",
                    "False poor", "Missed poor", "Misclassified"))
Index Cut-off Poor (%) Sensitivity Specificity False poor Missed poor Misclassified
Index A 4 0.188 0.803 0.967 0.027 0.039 0.066
Index B 4 0.175 0.644 0.942 0.047 0.071 0.118 
mis %>%
  select(index, `Wrongly classed as poor` = false_pos,
         `Poor missed by the index` = false_neg) %>%
  pivot_longer(-index, names_to = "error", values_to = "share") %>%
  ggplot(aes(index, share, fill = error)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), colour = "white", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#7f8c8d", "#2c3e50")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of the population misclassified", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

11 Summary

summary_tab <- data.frame(
  index         = names(pal),
  cfi           = fits$cfi.scaled[1:2],
  tli           = fits$tli.scaled[1:2],
  rmsea         = fits$rmsea.scaled[1:2],
  omega         = omega_tab$omega,
  r_sum_true    = cor_tab$r_sum_true,
  misclassified = mis$misclassified
)
kable(summary_tab, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Index", "CFI", "TLI", "RMSEA", "Omega",
                    "r (count, true)", "Misclassified"))
Index CFI TLI RMSEA Omega r (count, true) Misclassified
Index A 0.995 0.994 0.028 0.860 0.806 0.066
Index B 0.900 0.871 0.088 0.772 0.719 0.118
  • Index A: omega = 0.86, misclassification = 6.6%.
  • Index B: omega = 0.77, misclassification = 11.8%.
  • Two indices of the same length can differ widely in reliability. Report model fit, loadings, R² and omega together, and read them alongside the content of the items. None of them alone is enough to judge whether a count of deprivations can be trusted to identify the poor.
